Most early-stage teams are stuck hiring the same way: post a job, wait for applications, repeat. That cycle works for roles that attract a lot of inbound interest, but it leaves the majority of the qualified talent pool completely untouched: people who have jobs, aren’t browsing job boards, and aren’t responding to generic outreach. This guide covers how to reach those candidates through passive talent sourcing, from the tactics that actually move the needle to the infrastructure that keeps a passive pipeline from falling apart between searches.


**TLDR:**


-


Job boards reach only about 30% of the workforce; passive sourcing targets the other 70%.


-


Diversify beyond LinkedIn, which over half of hiring managers find oversaturated for passive outreach.


-


Referrals, personalized outreach, and employee-shared content each compound passive pipeline results over time.


-


Personalized candidate emails can increase role interest by 10-30% compared to generic outreach.


-


Some tools combine a free ATS with on-demand recruiting support at $2,000 to $7,000 per hire, no retainer required.


## What Is Passive Candidate Sourcing?


Passive candidate sourcing is the strategy of proactively targeting and engaging candidates who may be open to new opportunities but are not actively looking for a job. It typically involves identifying passive candidates through their digital footprints, from their LinkedIn profiles to their blogs, publications, and other digital properties, in order to start a conversation and inspire them to apply or interview for an open role.


### The Difference Between Active and Passive Candidates


Active candidates are job seekers who are actively looking for a new job and are taking steps to find one, such as submitting applications, networking, and attending job fairs. Passive candidates, on the other hand, are not actively looking for a new job but might be open to considering new opportunities if they arise.


Passive candidates might include people who are satisfied in their current job but are open to hearing about other opportunities, as well as those who are not actively looking for a job but might be open to considering one if the right opportunity comes along. They’re also more likely to be qualified candidates, or at least fit more of your requirements, since you’re seeking them out.


Active Candidates Passive Candidates


**Job-search status** Actively applying Working a job, not searching


**Where to reach them** Job boards, career fairs LinkedIn, GitHub, referrals, industry communities


**What motivates engagement** Finding any suitable role A compelling, specific opportunity


**Share of workforce** ~30% ~70%


**Typical fit level** Variable Often higher: you chose them based on criteria


## How to Find Passive Candidates


### 1. Make the Most of Social Media Platforms


Gone are the days of advertising on LinkedIn to find candidates. With 52% of hiring managers finding passive candidate hiring less effective due to LinkedIn being oversaturated, it may be beneficial to diversify your[recruitment source mix](https://www.dover.com/blog/sources-of-recruitment) beyond social alone.


Channel Best For Effort Level Typical Response Rate


LinkedIn Outreach Senior / professional roles Medium Low-Medium


GitHub / Dev Communities Engineering roles Medium-High Medium


Employee Referrals Culture-fit hires Low (once set up) High


Industry Slack / Forums Niche specialists Medium Medium-High


Content / Employer Brand Long-term pipeline High Compounding over time


And while most companies are on social, they’re not tapping into social media recruiting to its full potential. Here are a few ways to get started:


-


Post all jobs to social media. Or, at the very least, post that you’re hiring and consider promoting the post so candidates who come across your profile will know you’re actively recruiting.


-


Use hashtags to target specific audiences,especially for the roles you’re hiring for.


-


Share employer brand content. 48% of job seekers rank social media as the #1 place they go to research any “deal breakers” such as lower pay, less work-life balance, and lack of workplace flexibility. Post pictures of your team, or testimonials from staff members.


-


Post on behalf of recruiters’ social profiles. Or have recruiters create unique profiles for your company where they can recruit for their open reqs.


### 2. Invest in Automation Tools in Your Hiring Process


Automation is central to passive recruitment, and it’s key to providing an exceptional candidate experience in the passive sourcing process. In a competitive market, speed is everything.


Since passive talent isn’t actively looking, they won’t be motivated to respond unless you either have incredibly enticing recruiting emails or continuously nurture your relationship with them (similar to a sales prospect).[Automate candidate outreach](https://www.dover.com/blog/ats-automate-candidate-outreach-startup) tools, like Dover, can make sure you send timely follow-ups, create talent pools of candidates to reach out to later who responded “not yet”, and automate scheduling so you limit dropoff or losing out to other offers.


That automation works best when every candidate who enters the funnel – whether sourced through manual searches, outreach sequences, or referrals – flows into one shared ATS that both the recruiter and hiring team can see in real time. Without that shared system, follow-up gaps and duplicate outreach tend to surface, particularly when a[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-recruiter-guide) and an internal hiring manager are working the pipeline in parallel (see also[when a startup needs one](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-fractional-recruiter-when-startup-needs-one) ). The shared pipeline is the infrastructure that keeps sourcing at scale from breaking down. This is also the reason fractional recruiting agencies increasingly run on top of Dover: the ATS becomes the operating layer the agency delivers through, so every search builds on prior candidate history instead of starting cold.


### 3. Set Up a Referral Program


Referral-based recruiting has long been popular, and for a valid reason: widely cited research suggests roughly 78% of recruiters find their most fitting candidates through referrals from current employees.


To set up an employee referral program you’ll need to:


-


Create an outline of the rules of your program and document how it works. For example, you should think through: What kind of process do employees go through to make a referral? What kind of incentive is involved? How will you update your website with this added benefit?


-


Next, set up an incentive structure for referring successful new hires, such as bonuses or rewards.


-


Finally, track and monitor the efficacy of the referral program by reviewing metrics such as timing from when the person was referred to when they joined. A dedicated[referral tracking in your ATS](https://www.dover.com/blog/referral-tracking-ats-startups) setup makes this much easier to keep consistent over time.


## ‍How to Engage Passive Candidates


### 1. Stress Company Culture and Candidate Growth Potential


According to Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial[Survey](https://www.deloitte.com/global/en/issues/work/genz-millennial-survey.html) , younger workers are prioritizing stability, skills development, and well-being over fast-paced advancement, with just 25% of Gen Zs and 21% of millennials saying they prefer rapid career progression. This is especially true for passive candidates, who already have jobs and would need a compelling case beyond salary alone before making a move.


For passive candidates, outlining your company culture, making sure your employer brand is up to par, and outlining their growth potential are the most important things to convey in your initial outreach.


### 2. Send Personalized Sourcing Emails to Prospective Candidates


We’ve all seen the screenshots of mass recruiting emails gone wrong: using the wrong candidate name, or buggy personalization tokens that call out the wrong parts of a candidate’s profile. In a competitive recruiting market, candidates can tell what’s authentic from what’s not, and that’s why personalization matters.


With Dover, you can automatically generate personalized sentences for candidates using key skills that overlap with your role’s requirements. After analyzing more than 6,000 candidate touchpoints across personalized vs. non-personalized outreach, we found that personalization increased *interest* in a role by 10-30%. That’s even if the candidate responded as “not interested” to another company’s outreach.


And, even if a candidate isn’t actively looking to make a change, they’re more likely to keep you in mind for future career moves, meaning you’ll see increasing returns over time.


### 3. Build Employee Ambassadors and a Strong Brand in Your Industry


Employer branding doesn’t have to be a one-person job: enlist the help of eager team members or those with strong personal brands to promote your content on their personal profiles to see greater ROI. Content shared by employees receives[8x more engagement](https://nealschaffer.com/employee-advocacy-statistics/) than content shared by brand channels, which means you can more easily gain visibility over larger, more-recognized brands or competitors.


Though it may feel uncomfortable to ask employees to repost your content,[half of working Americans](https://www.careerarc.com/blog/employee-advocacy-social-media-survey/) say they’d be willing to share their company’s social media content to their own social channels. 30% of employees say they already have.


An easy way to solve this is to enlist different teams when the content is relevant to them: 24% of those surveyed say they would be more likely to share company social media if they had a direct connection to the content (i.e. it was related to the work they do)


And if you provide templated language for people to use or edit, they’re 27% more likely to post content to their personal profile.


A passive sourcing strategy built on all three of these pillars - consistent social presence, structured referrals, and employer brand amplification - tends to compound over time instead of resetting with each open role. ## FAQs


### What’s the difference between active and passive candidate sourcing strategies?


Active sourcing targets people who are already applying and browsing job boards, roughly 30% of the workforce. Passive sourcing reaches the other 70% through proactive outreach, referral programs, and employer brand content directed at working candidates who aren’t actively looking but may be open to the right opportunity.


### Should I use LinkedIn or diversify to other channels for passive candidate outreach?


Diversifying beyond LinkedIn is worth considering, since over half of hiring managers report that passive outreach on LinkedIn has become oversaturated. Platforms where your target candidates are professionally active (GitHub, Slack communities, niche industry forums) combined with employee-shared content and structured referral programs tend to produce better response rates for hard-to-fill roles.


### How does a shared ATS help with passive sourcing when a fractional recruiter is involved?


When a fractional recruiter and an internal hiring manager work from separate systems, follow-up gaps and duplicate outreach tend to surface, particularly with passive candidates who respond on their own timeline, sometimes weeks after initial contact. A shared ATS where both sides see the same candidate data in real time removes that coordination overhead and keeps warm leads from going cold between touchpoints.
